BFF win two honours at AFC Awards 2026 in Bangkok
item.description:
The Bangladesh Football Federation (BFF) secured two prestigious honours at the AFC Awards 2026 in Bangkok on Thursday, earning international recognition for its efforts to develop football across the country.
BFF won the AFC Member Association of the Year Award in the Ruby category and the AFC President's Recognition Award for Grassroots Football in the Silver category at the ceremony held in the Thai capital.
BFF Executive Committee member Md Golam Gaus received both awards on behalf of the federation.
The double recognition came after BFF was nominated in both categories this year, with the federation managing to convert both nominations into awards.
The Member Association of the Year Award recognises the overall development activities and achievements of AFC member associations. Its assessment covers international football performance, domestic competitions, grassroots development, coaching and refereeing programmes, women's football, social responsibility initiatives and football-related events.
The Grassroots Football award, meanwhile, acknowledges member associations' contributions to developing the game at the grassroots level. The evaluation considers development initiatives, competitions, social responsibility programmes, coaching courses and workshops, investment and other grassroots activities.
The latest achievement also means Bangladesh have received AFC grassroots recognition for the second consecutive year. BFF previously won the Bronze category of the AFC President's Recognition Award for Grassroots Football in 2025.
This year's success adds another significant honour through the Member Association category, marking a notable milestone for the country's football governing body.
In a statement, BFF described the two awards as a source of pride and inspiration for Bangladesh football, expressing hope that the recognition would further encourage its ongoing efforts to expand participation, strengthen grassroots development and build a sustainable football structure.
The federation said the recognition reflected its continued initiatives to develop the game at different levels across the country.

item.title: Malaysian gold medallist weightlifter loses arm in motorbike crash
item.description:
Commonwealth Games gold medallist weightlifter Mohd Hafizuddin Roslin had his right arm amputated after a serious motorcycle accident in his native Malaysia.
The 21-year-old was conscious and in a stable condition in hospital on Thursday, three days after the crash, the country's top weightlifting official said.
Hafizuddin won Commonwealth gold in the 88kg event in Glasgow in July and was a prospect for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.
"He is awake and smiling," Malaysia Weightlifting Federation president Ayub Rahmat told AFP.
"Physically his condition is improving but this incident has had a great impact on his future."
He called it "a shock and a huge loss" for weightlifting in the country.
Doctors amputated Hafizuddin's arm above the elbow, local media reports said.
The Malaysian government said it would cover all his treatment and medical costs.
"We are already looking at how he can be integrated into the sport, including a future coaching role in weightlifting," Ayub added.

item.title: Alcaraz reaches ATP Finals last four with help from Tiafoe
item.description:
Carlos Alcaraz reached the last four of the ATP Finals on Wednesday thanks to Frances Tiafoe after the Spaniard had earlier brushed aside world number five Daniil Medvedev 6-2, 6-4.
American Tiafoe beat Italian Flavio Cobolli 7-6 (8/6), 6-0 with his first set guaranteeing Alcaraz's spot in the next round.
Tiafoe kept his hopes of a semi-final spot alive in his maiden Finals appearance and faces Medvedev in his last group-stage match on Friday.
Seven-time Grand Slam champion Alcaraz needed just over 70 minutes to beat the Russian in Turin.
"A little bit of problems, you know, physically, in the match," Alcaraz said on-court after receiving some treatment in the second set.
"But I think everybody could see that I was able to still play good tennis, I could still move well."
By winning in straight sets, the 23-year-old will secure his spot in the semi-finals if Frances Tiafoe defeats Flavio Cobolli later or if the Italian beats the American in three sets.
Alcaraz has never won the season-ending Finals, finishing runner-up last year to Jannik Sinner.
But with Sinner injured and the Spaniard entering this season's edition on the back of a nine-match winning streak that earned him indoor titles in Vienna and at the Paris Masters, Alcaraz is considered the favourite to lift the trophy this year.
Since returning in August from a wrist injury that kept him off the tour for four months and prevented him from defending his French Open title, Alcaraz has won three of the five tournaments he has entered.
After easing past Tiafoe in his opener in Turin 6-2, 6-2, the third seed carried that ominous form into the first set against 2020 Finals winner Medvedev.
Alcaraz broke the Russian in successive games midway through the first frame to claim the opener.
He continued by breaking Medvedev in the very first game of the second set and proceeded to serve out, despite a brief stoppage to have his left thigh taped up.
"I didn't want to force myself to the limit physically. I was a break-up at that time. And I just tried to keep up my serve... play chill, smoothly, relaxed and just happy about it," Alcaraz said.
"So, I'm going to look at it with my team and I will see."
Medvedev, 30, is still in with a chance of advancing after winning his opening match against Cobolli in straight sets.
World number one Alexander Zverev is the man to beat in the John McEnroe Group and became the first player to book his spot in the semi-finals after beating Ben Shelton on Tuesday.

item.title: Pochettino calls for United to look beyond current struggles
item.description:
Mauricio Pochettino says it is a "mistake" to dwell on Manchester United's current plight, insisting the focus should be on the club's potential as he prepares for his first match in charge.
The Argentine takes his new team to bitter rivals Liverpool on Sunday -- just days after ending his reign as US coach.
United, who sacked Michael Carrick last week, are in the relegation zone after just one win in the Premier League this season.
Pochettino, speaking to in-house media in his first interview as United boss, said he wanted to free up his under-performing players.
"It's a mistake to see the (current) situation," he said. "We need to see the potential of this club. Of course, the circumstances are the circumstances, and we need to be responsible for the circumstances.
"But at the same time, we need to understand that it's a game and, to connect with the game, we need to feel free.
"The players need to express their talent, we need to create the environment and the platform for them to perform. That is the most important thing and that is the priority."
Pochettino will hold his first press conference as United manager on Friday.

item.title: Bangladesh to face Nepal in historic T20I at Lord's
item.description:
Bangladesh are set to make history at Lord's Cricket Ground when they take on Nepal in a men's T20 International on June 3, 2027, as part of the latter's tour of England.
The Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC) announced today that the iconic Home of Cricket will host the Bangladesh-Nepal encounter, marking the first time Bangladesh's men's team will play a T20 International at the historic venue.
The fixture will add to an eventful summer for Bangladesh cricket, with the national men's team scheduled to return to Lord's in late May for a Test match against England, their first appearance at the venue in 17 years.
Bangladesh will face Nepal on June 3, with a Middlesex T20 Blast fixture scheduled to take place later the same day. It will be the first time Lord's has hosted an international and domestic men's cricket double-header.
The match will be scheduled to accommodate television audiences in both countries, allowing cricket fans in Bangladesh and Nepal to follow the historic occasion live.
As part of MCC's hosting of Nepal's tour of England, Nepal will also play Ireland and Scotland in official international fixtures at Wormsley and Beckenham.
Tamim Iqbal, President of the Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB), described the occasion as a special moment for the national team and welcomed the opportunity to play at one of cricket's most prestigious venues.
"Playing at Lord's, the Home of Cricket, is a special occasion for the Bangladesh team and we are delighted to be part of this historic T20 International against Nepal in June 2027," Tamim said.
He noted that the match would mark the first men's T20 International appearance by Bangladesh at Lord's and make the team's return to the venue even more memorable following the Test against England after a 17-year gap.
Tamim also welcomed the opportunity for Bangladesh and Nepal supporters to share the occasion, while expressing appreciation to MCC and the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) for their support in arranging the fixture.
Bangladesh's women's team had earlier made its debut at Lord's against South Africa during the ICC Women's T20 World Cup in 2026.

item.title: South Africa crush Bangladesh by 9 wickets to take 1-0 lead
item.description:
South Africa stormed to a nine-wicket victory over Bangladesh in the first Test, riding on a stellar performance from left-arm spinner Simon Harmer at the Wanderers Stadium in Johannesburg today.
Harmer claimed 6-51 to bowl Bangladesh out for just 168 in their second innings on the final day, leaving South Africa with a modest target of 12 runs for victory.
Although opener Marques Ackerman, who smashed 157 in the first innings, fell for a duck after edging Mehidy Hasan Miraz to first slip, South Africa comfortably chased down the target in just nine deliveries.
Aiden Markram remained unbeaten on eight and struck the winning single to give South Africa a 1-0 lead in the two-match series.
Harmer was the chief architect of Bangladesh's second innings collapse, bamboozling the visitors with his guile and turn after they resumed the day at 100-5.
With defeat looming, Bangladesh managed to avoid an innings loss, thanks largely to a 47-run partnership between overnight batters Liton Das and Mushfiqur Rahim for the sixth wicket.
However, Kagiso Rabada broke the stand by bowling Liton for 39.
Mushfiqur and Mehidy Hasan Miraz then added 26 runs for the next wicket, further delaying South Africa's victory. But Harmer returned to trigger a dramatic collapse, claiming four of the last five wickets as Bangladesh lost their final four wickets for just eight runs.
Mushfiqur scored 22, while Miraz contributed 15.
Rabada finished with 3-48, adding to his first-innings haul of 5-70. His match figures of eight wickets earned him the Player of the Match award.
Earlier, Bangladesh posted an impressive 400 in their first innings, powered by Towhid Hridoy's 137, Liton Das's 120 and opener Tanzid Hasan Tamim's 67. The total marked the first instance of an Asian team scoring 400 in a first innings on South African soil.
South Africa responded emphatically, piling up 557 all out to establish a commanding 157-run first innings lead.
Ackerman led the charge with 157, while Ryan Rickelton scored 102. Jubayr Hamza contributed 83 and captain Temba Bavuma remained unbeaten on 68.

item.title: Combating the threat of cyber fraud
item.description:
As Bangladesh's economy becomes increasingly reliant on digital communication and financial transactions, the risks of cyber fraud are growing alongside it. Bangladesh Bank's latest directive asking banks to raise awareness among exporters about cyber threats is, therefore, a welcome step.
However, awareness alone will not be enough unless it is accompanied by stronger safeguards, accountability, and a more comprehensive approach to cybersecurity.
The central bank's warning highlights a particularly concerning threat: The manipulation of export documents and fraudulent changes to payment instructions. Such schemes can result in substantial financial losses, damage business relationships, and undermine confidence in Bangladesh's export sector.
With international trade increasingly dependent on electronic exchanges of information, even a seemingly minor lapse in communication security can have serious consequences.
The recommended precautions -- including independently verifying changes to banking details, avoiding suspicious links, and reporting suspected fraud promptly -- are practical measures that exporters must take seriously. Banks, meanwhile, have a responsibility to ensure that these warnings reach businesses of all sizes, particularly smaller exporters who may lack dedicated IT and cybersecurity teams.
But we must also recognize that cybercrime is not limited to export transactions. From online banking scams and identity theft to phishing attempts and the theft of personal financial information, ordinary citizens are increasingly exposed to digital threats.
Protecting the country's financial ecosystem requires a coordinated effort involving banks, regulators, law enforcement agencies, and technology providers.
Bangladesh Bank must ensure that its directive translates into meaningful action. Banks should invest in stronger security systems, regular staff training, effective fraud detection mechanisms, and accessible reporting channels. There must also be clear procedures for responding to cyber incidents and helping affected customers.
As we move towards a more digitally connected economy, cybersecurity cannot remain an afterthought. The cost of prevention is far lower than the financial and reputational damage caused by fraud, and we must build institutions capable of ensuring cybersecurity for our people and businesses.

item.title: Getting the nation under control
item.description:
The spread of arson attacks, crude bomb explosions, and political violence across Bangladesh is rapidly becoming a dangerous reality, and should serve as a serious warning to the authorities.
What began as a troubling pattern of incidents in Dhaka has now spread to other districts, with attacks on police stations, political leaders' homes, and vehicles. Most alarmingly, the violence in Faridpur claimed the life of a Krishak Dal leader who suffered severe burns.
This is a deeply disturbing situation that warrants nothing short of immediate and aggressive intervention.
The authorities need to recognize the urgency of getting the country under control before the situation deteriorates further. When people begin questioning whether they can safely travel, send their children to school, or go about their daily lives, it is clear that public confidence in security is being eroded.
The government must act on several fronts: Law enforcement agencies need to strengthen intelligence gathering, increase surveillance in vulnerable areas, and identify those organizing and financing these attacks.
Perpetrators must be brought to justice swiftly, but investigations must remain evidence-based. Political affiliations cannot become an excuse for selective enforcement, nor should innocent people become victims of indiscriminate action.
Political parties, too, must understand their responsibility. Provocative statements, threats, and attempts to mobilize supporters through intimidation will only deepen instability. No political objective can justify violence or the destruction of public and private property.
Bangladesh has already endured too much political turmoil to allow another prolonged period of insecurity to take hold. The government cannot afford to wait for the situation to spiral further before responding with the seriousness it deserves.
Restoring law and order is not a task that can be postponed or delegated to political parties; it is a fundamental responsibility of the state, and the authorities must demonstrate, urgently, that they remain firmly in control.

item.title: India: Online censorship grows after ‘Cockroach’ protests
item.description:
A video showing a young girl crying as she spoke about alleged police brutality during the youth-led Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protests in July. A video examining the Hindu nationalist Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh’s (RSS) contribution to the rise of India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). A satirical cartoon criticizing Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government.
These are among the examples of content that have recently been restricted on social media in India.
Content creator CitySavitri describes herself as a “nobody” in the world of social media. She had started making videos just two months ago and had around 600 followers on Instagram.
Yet a video looking at the RSS’s role in the BJP’s 2014 election victory was restricted in India within an hour of being posted. It was the first of three videos she posted that faced restrictions.
The experience made her feel that “anti-government commentary” was being monitored and curtailed.
“It is very plain and simple to understand,” the content creator told DW.
Independent journalist Sadhika Tiwari was covering the CJP protest in New Delhi on July 20, when police used batons and tear gas against demonstrators.
Tiwari’s video of a frightened young girl crying and speaking about police brutality garnered around 10 million views within hours, she said, before it was restricted in India.
Political cartoonist Satish Acharya has also faced repeated restrictions, with Instagram blocking his profile twice recently.
In May 2025, during the conflict between India and Pakistan, independent digital news outlet Maktoob Media’s X account was withheld in India while it was reporting on the escalating crisis, its founder and editor Aslah Kayyalakkath told DW.
“We received no official notice or email from either the government or X. It was our readers who first alerted us to the blocking,” he said.
Maktoob Media said it contacted Indian officials and X but received no response. Access to the account was restored a few days later, again without an explanation.
Kayyalakkath said Maktoob’s content from the July protest also faced restrictions. “Suppressing independent journalism undermines transparency, accountability and democratic values,” he said.
Several of the content creators and journalists interviewed by DW said they received no prior notification or explanation for the restrictions.
Some users were not sure if their content had been blocked at the government’s request or proactively by the social media platforms.
When asked for comment, Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, pointed DW to a website statement noting users can appeal content and account restrictions.
At the heart of the debate are India’s IT Rules, 2021, amended in February 2026. Section 79 of India’s IT Act protects social media platforms and other intermediaries from liability for content posted by third parties, provided they meet certain legal conditions.
One such requirement, introduced through the February 2026 amendments, is to remove or disable access to specified unlawful content within three hours of receiving a valid court order or a reasoned government notice. The previous deadline was 36 hours.
Failure to comply can result in intermediaries losing their liability protection.
The government’s Sahyog portal, which coordinates takedown requests between law enforcement, platforms and telecom providers, has faced criticism over the pace at which notices are issued.
Meta said it uses automated tools and technologies to detect and review content that may violate its community standards. It also automatically restricts access to certain types of content in India to comply with legal requirements under the IT rules.
Pranesh Prakash, a technology law and policy adviser, said the amended rules allow authorized police officials to notify intermediaries about content they consider unlawful without necessarily filing a formal complaint or initiating other legal proceedings.
“This has led to the worst period of social media censorship that India has ever seen, with digital news media accounts being blocked, cartoonists’ accounts being blocked, and even mere discussions of an opposition leader’s memoirs being blocked,” he said. “Clearly, none of these disclosed any ‘unlawful acts.’”
Prakash also raised concerns about the lack of public information on government requests to remove content, saying this made it difficult to assess the scale of restrictions.
The Software Freedom Law Center, India (SFLC.in), a digital rights organization, said the growing reliance on automated takedowns raised serious concerns about transparency, accountability and due process.
“There is little transparency about the processes through which content is identified, flagged and restricted, or whether there is any meaningful human oversight before a takedown is implemented,” SFLC.in told DW.
The organization also tested X’s verification process by submitting a takedown request against one of its own posts using a fake email address. X registered the request, raising questions about how it verified the identity and authority of those submitting requests.
After SFLC.in alerted the company, X introduced email verification codes for people submitting takedown requests.
“A channel that lets anyone pose as a law enforcement official can be misused to silence lawful speech,” SFLC.in said.
X did not respond to DW’s request for a comment.
The Indian government denies that it is censoring online content.
While the ministry did not respond to DW’s latest request for a comment, in an email response to DW in August, Vinod Kumar, chief of media and communications at the Information Technology Ministry, said Instagram posts by students and protesters following the July CJP protests “are not being taken down as alleged.”
“Media enjoys freedom in India. The Government does not censor online content,” Kumar said, adding that the government only acts against “objectionable content.”
Under the Indian IT rules, “unlawful content” generally refers to material which could threaten India’s sovereignty and integrity, disturb public order, incite violence, or constitute defamation.
However, social media influencers such as university professor Madri Kakoti, alias Dr Medusa, continue to report restrictions. Kakoti’s Instagram account was restricted in India on November 16 without notice, she said, along with that of satirist Shamita Yadav.
Rights groups including Human Rights Watch have warned that expanding content restrictions could chill free expression and encourage self-censorship among journalists, creators and ordinary users.
Acharya, however, said he would continue his work.
“The Indian Constitution gives me the right to draw political cartoons,” he said. “It’s totally democratic to question and criticize the government in India.”
For Tiwari, the issue goes beyond the reach of a single video. It is also about preserving a record of what happened, after the Delhi Police denied allegations of using excessive force during the July 20 protest in front of the Supreme Court.
“We have seen several other videos now, and it’s well established why that girl was crying, and that the Delhi Police used force and lied about it,” she said.
“Still, I want that video back up because it needs to stay for posterity. I think that’s the larger idea: they want to take this stuff down so it fades from memory, allowing them to categorically deny it later when we have little left to show for what happened.”

ULAB cricket team honoured after winning ABG University Cup 2026
item.description:
The University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB) cricket team was honoured at a reception on Wednesday after winning the ABG University Cup 2026.
The reception was held at the ULAB Cricket Ground, where the university authorities congratulated the players on their achievement.
Addressing the event, ULAB Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr Shamsad Mortuza said the team's victory was a matter of pride for the university, attributing the success to the players' collective effort, dedication and perseverance.
ULAB Treasurer Professor Dr Milan Kumar Bhattacharjee said the championship reflected the talent, leadership and competitive spirit of the university's students.
Registrar Lt Col Md Foyzul Islam (Retd) said the victory would inspire greater enthusiasm for sports among students and encourage them to achieve further success.
Commemorative crests were presented to each member of the winning team, along with the coach and team manager, in recognition of their performance. Faculty members, university officials and students also attended the reception.
The ABG University Cup 2026 featured 10 private universities from across the country. ULAB remained unbeaten in the group stage, winning all four matches to secure eight points and qualify for the semi-finals as group champions.
In the semi-final, ULAB defeated Fareast International University by 81 runs to reach the final.
The final was held on November 13 at Anvir Cricket Stadium in Bashundhara Sports City, where ULAB defeated Sonargaon University by 53 runs to secure the title.
Batting first, ULAB scored 205 for two in 20 overs, powered by Farhan's unbeaten 109 off 61 balls. In reply, Sonargaon University managed 152 runs, giving ULAB a 53-run victory.

item.title: SC to hear appeal over postponed university admission tests Nov 23
item.description:
The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court (SC) on Thursday set November 23 for hearing a state appeal against a High Court order postponing admission tests at all public universities across the country, including Dhaka University, until December 31.
Appellate Division Judge-in-Chamber Justice Md Rezaul Haque passed the order, forwarding the matter to the apex court full bench for hearing.
A High Court division bench comprising Justice Ahmed Sohel and Justice SM Iftekhar Uddin Mahamud passed the initial order on Wednesday, after holding hearing on a writ petition filed by Supreme Court lawyer Advocate Quamrun Nahar Mahmud.
Attorney General Barrister Md Ruhul Quddus Kazal took part in the hearing for state on Thursday, while Adv Qazi Mohammad Joynal Abedin appeared for Dhaka University and Advocate Mahbubur Rahman Khan for University Grants Commission.

item.title: Majid Majidi’s ‘Midday Meal’ wins top prize at Busan film festival
item.description:
Iranian filmmaker Majid Majidi's drama “Midday Meal” has won the top prize at the 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) in South Korea, securing automatic eligibility for the Academy Awards' International Feature Film category.
The film follows a teacher in a poor Iranian village who turns to smuggling to keep his school running. It was selected as the winner by a jury led by Chinese filmmaker Zhang Yimou, known for “Raise the Red Lantern”.
Accepting the award on Thursday, Majidi paid tribute to his mother, saying her love and energy had inspired him before her death a few months ahead of the film's production.
He also praised the Iranian people for their resilience amid ongoing conflict with the United States, years of economic sanctions and limited access to medicine.
The win carries added significance following changes to the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences' Oscar eligibility rules introduced in May. Under the revised system, films winning top awards at six recognized international festivals, including Busan, Cannes and Berlin, can qualify directly for consideration in the International Feature Film category.
Previously, each country could submit only one film, selected by an Academy-approved committee. The eligible entries are subsequently narrowed down to five nominees.
The Busan festival introduced its first competitive section in 2025, with this year's competition featuring 13 films, including three South Korean productions.
Beyond the competition, the festival recognized several prominent figures in international cinema. Oscar-winning actress Michelle Yeoh received the Asian Filmmaker of the Year award, while Hong Kong filmmaker Ann Hui was presented with the Camellia Award for her contributions to empowering women in the film industry.
The 31st edition opened with South Korean director Kim Jong-kwan's drama “The Table: Day and Night”. Organizers said the festival screened 315 films, including 246 officially selected titles, marking its largest lineup since 2019.
More than 200,000 visitors attended this year's festival, according to the organizers.

Directed by Arif Khan and produced by Anonna Ruma, the special program is scheduled to air on Channel i on November 17 at 10:15 pm.

item.title: Shiv Shambho: The sound that defined Durga Puja 2026 in Bangladesh
item.description:
Every Durga Puja has its own soundtrack. The familiar beats of the dhak, the sound of conch shells, and the chants of Chandi Path are inseparable from the celebrations.
Yet every year, there are also songs that find a special place in the festivities, becoming part of the collective memories of those who celebrate.
During Durga Puja 2026 in Bangladesh, one such composition was “Shiv Shambho” by Mithun Chakra.
Featuring Mithun Chakra, Pantha Kanai and Animes Roy, the song brought an ancient devotional tradition into a contemporary musical setting.
At mandaps across the country and at Puja concerts in Dhaka and Chittagong, its rhythms became part of the celebrations, drawing people into a shared experience of music, movement and devotion.
What makes the composition particularly interesting, however, is the philosophy behind its invocation. Inspired by a hymn attributed to Sage Ved Vyasa, “Shiv Shambho” explores ideas that go beyond religious ritual: the relationship between nothingness and creation, silence and sound, and the unmanifest and the manifest.
Mithun Chakra wrote the lyrics, composed the melody, arranged the music, and performed as a vocalist. The music was produced by Sohag Chakraborty, while HM Sohel directed the video. For Mithun, the composition is more than a song; it is a realization.
Its reception during Durga Puja raises an interesting question about devotional music in contemporary cultural life: can a composition be both an expression of spiritual contemplation and a source of collective celebration? “Shiv Shambho” offers an opportunity to explore how the two can coexist.
Durga Puja in Bangladesh is as much a celebration of community and cultural identity as it is an expression of faith.
Across Dhaka and the country’s towns and villages, mandaps become gathering places where generations come together through rituals, music, art and shared traditions.
Beneath the festivities, however, lies a deeper spiritual significance. The moments of prayer, the recitation of sacred texts, and the contemplation of the Goddess are reminders of the philosophical traditions that have shaped the festival over centuries.
Although Durga Puja celebrates Goddess Durga, the relationship between Shiva and Shakti is central to understanding the broader spiritual philosophy of Sanatan Dharma.
In this philosophical understanding, Shiva represents consciousness, stillness, and the unmanifest, while Shakti represents the dynamic energy through which creation takes place.
Their relationship speaks to the interconnectedness of consciousness and creative energy. Shiva represents the stillness underlying existence, while Shakti is the force through which existence finds expression.
Seen in this context, invoking Shiva during Durga Puja is not separate from celebrating Shakti. Rather, it draws attention to the spiritual relationship between the two.
What makes “Shiv Shambho” particularly compelling is that it brings these ideas into a musical experience without separating devotion from celebration. People can dance to its rhythm while engaging with the spiritual meaning of its words.
Devotion does not necessarily have to be expressed through silence or solemnity; it can also find expression through music, movement, and collective joy.
The name “Shiv Shambho” offers an opportunity to explore a particularly fascinating philosophical idea.
One interpretation understands Shiv as nothing. This is not “nothing” in the ordinary sense of emptiness or absence, but a primordial state beyond form, identity, and manifestation. It is the stillness that precedes creation, beyond the distinctions through which we ordinarily understand existence.
Shambhu, meanwhile, is associated with auspiciousness and benevolence. The philosophical interpretation of Shambhu emerging from Shiv suggests that auspiciousness and creation arise from this primordial nothingness.
In Mithun’s words, “Shiv represents the formless, while Shambho is the primordial sound—the universe manifesting itself. To me, ‘Shiv Shambho’ is not merely a song; it is an invocation, a manifestation of these two words.”
“It is like a mystical elixir: when you surrender to it without preconceived notions or expectations, something miraculous happens. A kind of magic unfolds. It is not about singing or listening to music; it is about an exchange of energy.”
It is an idea that invites us to look at existence differently. We often think of creation as the beginning of something tangible, something that can be seen or experienced. But what if everything begins with something that has no form? What if the source of creation is a state of stillness that exists beyond our ability to define it?
In this understanding, Shiv is the unmanifest, while Shambhu represents the emergence of auspiciousness from that unmanifest state. It is a movement from nothingness towards manifestation, from stillness towards expression.
This also brings us back to Shiva and Shakti. If Shiva represents primordial consciousness, Shakti is the dynamic energy through which existence finds expression. The relationship between the two offers a way of understanding how creation emerges from the unmanifest.
Perhaps this is what makes the philosophy so meaningful beyond its religious context. Amid the constant movement, noise, and demands of everyday life, the idea of returning to an underlying stillness offers an opportunity for reflection.
The invocation of “Shiv Shambho” can therefore be understood not only as an expression of devotion, but also as a reminder of the relationship between stillness, creation and transformation.
The relationship between sound and creation is another important aspect of Sanatan philosophy.
The concept of Nada Brahma, often understood as the idea that sound is a manifestation of the ultimate reality, offers an interesting perspective on the role of music in spiritual practice. Sound is not merely something we hear; it can also be a means of contemplating and experiencing the divine.
There is a natural connection here with the philosophy of “Shiv Shambho.” If Shiv represents primordial stillness, sound can be understood as an expression of the movement from silence towards manifestation. The emergence of sound from silence offers a beautiful parallel to the idea of creation emerging from the unmanifest.
This is also why chanting occupies such an important place in devotional traditions.
The repetition of a divine name, known as japa, is a meditative practice through which the mind is directed towards a single point of focus. Chanting Shiva’s name can be an expression of faith, a means of cultivating inner stillness, or an opportunity to reconnect with one’s spiritual beliefs.
When people chant together, the experience takes on another dimension. Individual voices merge into a shared rhythm, creating a sense of belonging and participation. What begins as a personal expression of devotion becomes something an entire gathering can experience.
This helps explain the enduring appeal of devotional music. It can be deeply personal while bringing people together.
In the case of “Shiv Shambho,” the musical arrangement invites movement and participation, while the invocation itself leaves room for contemplation. The two experiences are not contradictory. Spirituality can find expression through both silence and celebration.
Religious music has always evolved alongside the communities that sustain it. Hymns, kirtans, folk compositions and classical devotional traditions have travelled across generations, adapting to different musical forms while retaining the ideas that gave them meaning.
Contemporary devotional music continues this process. Digital platforms and changing listening habits have made it possible for traditional compositions and new interpretations of ancient texts to reach audiences far beyond the spaces in which they originated.
In Bangladesh, where music, language, literature, and religious traditions contribute to a rich cultural heritage, this evolution is particularly significant. Contemporary artistic expressions can provide younger generations with opportunities to engage with inherited traditions in ways that feel accessible without losing their philosophical depth.
A composition inspired by an ancient hymn but presented through a contemporary musical arrangement can create precisely this connection. It allows an old devotional idea to find a new audience while keeping its spiritual origins in view.
The presence of “Shiv Shambho” during this year’s Puja illustrates how devotional music can move between different spaces: from personal listening to public celebrations, and from individual reflection to collective participation.
Music also plays an important role in how festivals are remembered. Durga Puja is a time of reunions, family gatherings and renewed friendships. Every year brings its own experiences, and certain songs inevitably become associated with particular moments.
A melody heard at a mandap or during a concert can, years later, bring back memories of the people, places and celebrations surrounding it.
The ways in which people experience music have changed, from cassette recordings and neighborhood loudspeakers to digital releases and streaming platforms. Yet music continues to shape the emotional identity of festivals.
Whether “Shiv Shambho” becomes a lasting part of the collective memory of Durga Puja 2026 remains to be seen. Its significance will ultimately depend not only on how widely it is heard, but also on the experiences and meanings listeners associate with it.
No single composition can capture everything that Durga Puja means to people in Bangladesh. Every community and mandap has its own traditions and ways of celebrating. Yet a song can sometimes capture a particular feeling of a festival in ways that words alone cannot.
The significance of “Shiv Shambho” lies in its ability to bring together an ancient devotional tradition and contemporary cultural expression. It offers a reminder that devotion can inspire both reflection and joy.
Perhaps the most compelling idea behind the invocation is that auspiciousness emerges from nothingness, that the unmanifest gives rise to the manifest, and that stillness can be the beginning of creation.
In that sense, “Shiv Shambho” is more than another devotional composition in the soundscape of Durga Puja. It is also an invitation to reflect on the philosophy that gives the invocation its meaning.
It does not replace the dhak, the conch shells, or the centuries-old chants that have long been part of the festival. Instead, it adds another voice to a tradition that continues to find new ways of expressing itself.
And when the lights have been switched off, the mandaps have emptied, and the idols have been immersed, perhaps what remains is the sounds that made us feel connected to something larger than ourselves.

item.title: UN expert: Bangladesh cannot bear Rohingya burden indefinitely
item.description:
The international community must not expect Bangladesh to shoulder the Rohingya refugee crisis indefinitely or alone, and has a moral responsibility to pursue lasting political solutions rather than relying solely on humanitarian assistance, UN human rights expert Kelley E Currie has said.
Currie, the UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar, said the international community had a “100% moral obligation” to help Bangladesh, which continues to host more than a million Rohingya refugees amid declining humanitarian funding and deteriorating security conditions across the border.
Concluding her 8-day visit to Bangladesh, Currie spoke to Dhaka Tribune Chief Reporter Ali Asif Shawon about prospects for Rohingya repatriation, abuses by Myanmar’s military and the Arakan Army, accountability mechanisms, and the need for a political settlement that would allow refugees to return home with full rights.
UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar Kelley E Currie speaks to Dhaka Tribune during her visit to Bangladesh. Photo: Abir Ahmmed Shupto/Dhaka Tribune
Kelley E Currie: The situation is extremely difficult. Fighting between Myanmar’s military and the Arakan Army remains intense, particularly in northern Rakhine, where most Rohingya originate.
The Arakan Army has imposed severe restrictions on Rohingya communities. They are also caught between the Arakan Army and Rohingya armed groups aligned with the military regime. Both sides are forcibly recruiting people, and neither is particularly favourable towards the Rohingya.
However, I believe Myanmar could eventually become a federal democratic state that respects everyone’s rights. Some resistance organisations have expressed openness to Rohingya returning with full citizenship, land ownership, education and equal participation in society.
Ultimately, there is no military solution. A political settlement and a change of hearts and minds are essential. Some dialogue is already taking place, which gives me hope.
But progress will remain extremely difficult while the military regime continues exploiting hostility towards the Rohingya.
Several accountability processes are underway, including cases before the International Court of Justice, International Criminal Court, courts in Argentina and other national jurisdictions.
The UN’s Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar is collecting extensive evidence, including documentation of the 2017 atrocities and violations committed by non-state actors. This evidence is essential for future prosecutions.
However, accountability also requires transitional justice, which cannot succeed without a political settlement.
My goal is to see Myanmar itself prosecute perpetrators and deliver justice to victims. That would be the best form of accountability, although we remain some distance from achieving it.
The international community has a 100% moral obligation.
Many countries have provided substantial humanitarian assistance, but they must think more seriously about durable solutions.
There should be no expectation that Bangladesh will bear this burden indefinitely or alone.
Bangladesh faces immense challenges of its own, including economic setbacks and political difficulties. The international community must ensure the country has at least a fighting chance.
That responsibility goes beyond humanitarian funding. It requires sustained political engagement, greater emphasis on human rights and dialogue, and the inclusion of marginalised voices in discussions about Myanmar’s future.
The international community must make that political effort rather than relying on armed solutions or humanitarian assistance alone.
Myanmar’s military authorities have said they are not ready to allow my visit. But the regime does not control the entire country and is not recognised by the UN as its legitimate government.
We are exploring alternative approaches, although some discussions are too sensitive to disclose.
I intend to request access again in January and engage neighbouring countries that may have influence.
Meanwhile, Myanmar’s civil society organisations are doing remarkable work documenting abuses despite security threats, restricted internet access and other obstacles.
Their evidence-gathering efforts remain crucial to accountability.
I am developing recommendations for Bangladesh, the UN system and international donors.
One priority is to strengthen social cohesion and create opportunities for both Rohingya refugees and host communities in Cox’s Bazar.
Rather than operating isolated programs, assistance should strengthen existing systems and benefit everyone.
Refugees should have greater opportunities for education, skills development and constructive community activities.
For example, they could receive training to organise fire brigades or repair water infrastructure. These skills would also help them rebuild their lives after returning home.
At the same time, investments must deliver lasting benefits to host communities. The water system developed through cooperation between the World Bank and Bangladesh is a good example.
We need more coordinated interventions that strengthen entire communities rather than treating refugees and local residents separately.

item.title: Ex-MP Haji Rahim Ullah's ancestral home looted, set fire in Feni
item.description:
Unidentified miscreants looted and set fire to the ancestral residence of former Feni-3 member of parliament Haji Rahim Ullah at Sonapur village in Sonagazi upazila of Feni early Thursday.
Rahim Ullah’s brother-in-law Rafiqul Islam, who was alone in the house, said 15 to 20 armed miscreants scaled the wall, looted valuable belongings, and poured petrol to set fire to three rooms of the multi-story house and three trucks parked outside.
Local residents rushed to the spot and managed to bring the flames under control, said Sonagazi Fire Service Acting Station Officer Md. Nurul Alam.
Sonagazi Model Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Abul Hashim said police visited the scene.
Haji Rahim Ullah is a former president of the Jeddah chapter of the Awami League. He was elected MP from Feni-3 constituency as an independent candidate in the 10th parliamentary election in 2014.
He has been in jail since his arrest in Dhaka’s Dhanmondi area in October 2024.

item.title: AB Party chairman’s car set ablaze in Bijoynagar
item.description:
Miscreants set fire to the parked car of Amar Bangladesh (AB) Party Chairman Mujibur Rahman Manju in the capital’s Bijoynagar early Thursday.
The incident took place at around 3am beneath the party’s central office, said Azadul Islam Azad, the party’s assistant publicity secretary, in a statement.
According to the party, several masked men arrived in an autorickshaw, poured an inflammable substance from a bottle over Manju’s parked car and set it on fire before fleeing the scene.
The party’s night guards spotted the incident on CCTV cameras and rushed to extinguish the flames. However, part of the vehicle had already been damaged.
In a joint statement issued on Thursday, AB Party Senior Vice-Chairman Professor Dr Major (retd) Abdul Wahab Minar and General Secretary Barrister Asaduzzaman Fuad condemned the attack.
They said setting fire to a political party chairman’s car in the middle of the night was not an isolated incident but a direct assault on political tolerance, democratic values and the country’s political environment.
The leaders said such cowardly attacks and acts of terrorism would not intimidate or silence the AB Party. They added that resorting to arson would only further alienate fascist forces from the people.
They also alleged that the ousted fascist forces had carried out the attack as part of an attempt to destabilise the country.
Describing arson, attacks and intimidation as unacceptable means of suppressing political opponents, they urged the government to take a firm stance against such crimes to protect the country’s democratic environment and political stability.
The two leaders called on law enforcement agencies to conduct a thorough investigation, analyse CCTV footage, identify and arrest those responsible, and ensure exemplary punishment.

item.title: ILO urges dialogue to end RMG wage unrest
item.description:
The International Labour Organization (ILO) has urged the government, garment manufacturers and workers’ representatives to resolve the ongoing minimum wage dispute in Bangladesh’s ready-made garment (RMG) sector through evidence-based negotiations and sustained dialogue.
In a statement issued on Thursday, the ILO said it was closely monitoring the wage review and related unrest, expressing concern over reports of violence, vandalism and disruptions affecting workers, businesses and industrial relations.
The organisation welcomed the government’s formation of the Minimum Wage Board, describing consultation among employers and workers as essential to a credible wage-setting process.
Citing the ILO Minimum Wage Fixing Convention, 1970 (No 131), it said wage adjustments should be transparent and based on reliable data, taking into account workers’ living costs, inflation, productivity, employment and the sustainability of businesses.
The ILO also stressed the importance of respecting freedom of association, workers’ right to organise and collective bargaining. It urged all parties to pursue peaceful means to ease tensions and allow the Minimum Wage Board to complete its work.
The organisation reaffirmed its commitment to supporting Bangladesh through technical assistance, research and social dialogue, including efforts to develop an evidence-based, gender-responsive National Wage Policy.

item.title: President: Bangladesh achieves remarkable success in agriculture
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Thursday said Bangladesh has achieved remarkable success in agriculture.
"Although the country faced a huge deficit in food grains immediately after independence, Bangladesh has now been able to increase agricultural production manifold. There is no overall food grain deficit in the country, thanks to the farmers, agricultural scientists and researchers," he said.
The president said this when a delegation from Khulna Agricultural University, led by its Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr Md Asaduzzaman Sarker, paid a courtesy call on him at Bangabhaban, said a press release issued by the President's Press Wing.
The president said just after independence, Bangladesh had a population of around 7.5 crore and faced a huge deficit in food grains. "Bangladesh, once known as a food-deficit country, has now been able to increase agricultural production manifold," he said.
The delegation informed the president that Khulna Agricultural University had been able to produce various climate-resilient food crops in the southern region despite several adverse conditions, including climate change and salinity.
During the meeting, the president stressed the effective field-level application of research-based technologies, safe food production and environment-friendly agricultural practices to build a sustainable agricultural system.
He also called for closer coordination among agricultural education, research and extension activities.
At the meeting, the vice-chancellor briefed the president on the university's academic and research activities and its overall progress and invited the president to attend the university's upcoming convocation ceremony. The president accepted the invitation and assured the delegation of his presence at the event.
The President's Military Secretary, Secretary and Press Secretary, along with Treasurer and Registrar of Khulna Agricultural University, were also present.
